summary: Penicillin V (phenoxymethylpenicillin) is an acid-stable, orally administered natural penicillin used to treat mild to moderate infections caused by susceptible organisms, predominantly streptococci. It is the oral drug of choice for streptococcal pharyngitis (group A strep) and is used for skin and soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible streptococci, mild erysipelas, and oral/dental infections, as well as for prophylaxis against rheumatic fever and for pneumococcal prophylaxis in patients with asplenia or sickle cell disease. It inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, leading to cell lysis. Its spectrum is narrow and it is destroyed by beta-lactamases, so it is not effective against penicillinase-producing staphylococci or most Gram-negative organisms. It is generally well tolerated; the most important risks are hypersensitivity reactions (ranging from rash to anaphylaxis) and gastrointestinal effects including Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Because absorption is reduced by food, it is best taken on an empty stomach. There is cross-reactivity in patients allergic to other penicillins.
indications: Mild to moderate streptococcal infections, including pharyngitis/tonsillitis and skin/soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible group A streptococci
Mild to moderately severe pneumococcal respiratory tract infections (e.g., otitis media) caused by susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae
Mild infections of the oral cavity (e.g., Vincent's gingivitis) and fusospirochetosis
Prophylaxis of recurrent rheumatic fever and/or chorea
Prophylaxis against pneumococcal infection in patients with asplenia or sickle cell disease

Adjust dose and duration to infection and severity

moa: Penicillin V is a beta-lactam antibiotic that exerts a bactericidal effect by inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis. It binds to and inactivates penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), the transpeptidase enzymes that catalyze the cross-linking of peptidoglycan strands in the bacterial cell wall. Inhibition of cross-linking weakens the cell wall, and ongoing autolytic enzyme activity leads to cell lysis and death, particularly in actively dividing organisms. Its phenoxymethyl side chain confers acid stability, allowing oral absorption, but it remains susceptible to hydrolysis by bacterial beta-lactamases (penicillinases), which limits its activity against penicillinase-producing organisms such as most Staphylococcus aureus.

absolute: History of serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reaction) to penicillins
relative: History of allergy to cephalosporins or other beta-lactams (possible cross-reactivity)
History of significant atopy/asthma (increased risk/severity of allergic reactions)
Phenylketonuria for products containing aspartame (check formulation)
monitor: Gastrointestinal symptoms, including persistent or bloody diarrhea (C. difficile)
Clinical response and resolution of infection
Renal function with prolonged or high-dose use

preg: Penicillins, including penicillin V, are generally considered safe in pregnancy and are widely used when indicated; no clear evidence of fetal harm has been established. Use during pregnancy when a penicillin is appropriate for the infection being treated.
lact: Penicillin V is excreted into breast milk in small amounts and is considered compatible with breastfeeding. Observe the breastfed infant for potential effects such as diarrhea, candidiasis (thrush), or rash, and report any allergic-type reactions.
renal: Penicillin V is eliminated largely by the kidneys. In patients with significant renal impairment, prolong the dosing interval (reduce frequency) rather than necessarily lowering each dose, and monitor renal function. No adjustment is generally required for mild impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is usually required for hepatic impairment. Use with caution in severe hepatic dysfunction and monitor clinically.

major: Other beta-lactam antibiotics in patients with penicillin allergy - risk of cross-hypersensitivity
moderate: Probenecid - decreases renal tubular secretion of penicillin, raising and prolonging serum penicillin levels
Bacteriostatic antibiotics (e.g., tetracyclines, chloramphenicol) - may theoretically antagonize the bactericidal action of penicillin
Methotrexate - penicillins may reduce its renal clearance and increase toxicity
Oral contraceptives - rare reports of reduced efficacy; advise additional precautions if concerned
minor: May reduce the efficacy of typhoid (oral live) vaccine - separate administration
interactions.food: Food reduces absorption; take on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals).
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction with alcohol; moderate intake is acceptable.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urine glucose tests with copper-reduction (Clinitest) methods; can transiently affect some serologic tests. Use enzymatic glucose tests.

rare: Seizures (very high doses, especially with renal failure)
emergency: Anaphylaxis (difficulty breathing, throat/face swelling, hives, collapse)

monitoring: Clinical response and resolution of the infection; complete the full course
Signs of hypersensitivity, both immediate and delayed, during therapy
Gastrointestinal tolerance and any persistent or bloody diarrhea suggestive of C. difficile

Complete blood count with prolonged therapy
counsel: Take this antibiotic on an empty stomach (about an hour before or two hours after eating) for best effect, and space doses evenly
Finish the entire course even if you feel better, to fully clear the infection and prevent resistance
Tell your doctor before starting if you have ever had an allergic reaction to penicillin or related antibiotics
Stop the medicine and seek urgent help if you develop a rash, itching, swelling, or difficulty breathing
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea, which can occur during or even weeks after treatment
Shake liquid forms well, keep refrigerated, and discard after the time stated on the label
pk: Absorbed within ~30-60 minutes; antibacterial effect begins shortly after
Peak serum concentration ~30-60 minutes after an oral dose
Therapeutic levels maintained with dosing every 6-8 hours
Store tablets at room temperature; refrigerate reconstituted suspension (2-8 C) and discard after ~14 days
pearls: Oral drug of choice for group A streptococcal pharyngitis and for secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever; acid-stable so it can be given by mouth
Narrow spectrum and beta-lactamase-labile - NOT reliable against most S. aureus or Gram-negative organisms; use a beta-lactamase-stable agent when staphylococci are likely
Take on an empty stomach for optimal absorption
Probenecid raises and prolongs penicillin levels by blocking tubular secretion (occasionally used therapeutically)
Cross-reactivity with other penicillins (and some cephalosporins) - take a careful allergy history; anaphylaxis is the most feared reaction
Prolong the dosing interval in significant renal impairment; very high doses in renal failure can rarely cause seizures
missed: If you miss a dose of penicillin V, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule - do not take a double dose. Try to keep doses evenly spaced.
overdose: Penicillin V has a wide margin of safety. Overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; in patients with severe renal impairment, very high serum levels can rarely cause neuromuscular irritability or seizures. Treatment is supportive and symptomatic; penicillin can be removed by hemodialysis if necessary in severe renal failure.
